General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Indiewire ↗ Open Full Page

From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2648 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jimmy Stewart once said that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.
  • Emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography.
  • According to recent reports, clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jimmy Stewart once said that with movies, it’s key moments that people remember.

Emily Blunt, who’s on the circuit these days talking about her standout role as a language-spouting meteorologist in Steven Spielberg’s “Disclosure Day,” gave me some memorable scenes that she will never forget from her wide-ranging filmography. (We spoke on Zoom.).

According to recent reports, clearly, Blunt can deliver in any genre: romance, comedy, musical, sci-fi, action, thriller, drama. So far, Blunt has notched one Oscar nomination, for Supporting Actress in Christopher Nolan’s bio-drama “Oppenheimer.” Sci-fi thriller “Disclosure Day” could score Blunt’s first Best Actress nod. (More below.) Related Stories How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder Super Bowl LXI to Play Live on IMAX Screens.

Recent findings suggest that 1. “My Summer of Love” (2005, Pawel Pawlikowski) was Blunt’s first movie role. “I remember the wildness of that Edith Piaf dance [‘La Foule’], where I have the cigarette dangling out of my mouth, and she’s trying to romanticize this girl from the wrong side of town and sophisticate her. I remember the scene with Paddy Considine where she tries to seduce him and then she laughs at him. I will never forget the energy in that room and how Paddy was in that scene. I have taken what Pawel taught me about ambiguity and reality on camera, and I have used it throughout my career. I am an untrained actor. I don’t have anything technical to fall back on, but the aliveness that he created on ‘My Summer of Love’ was informative for how I moved forward: what lies beneath the character. You know what the front foot is, and what is the shadow of that person? What’s really going on?”.

According to recent reports, 2. “The Devil Wears Prada“ (2006, David Frankel) marked Blunt’s Hollywood breakout as Miranda Priestley’s beleaguered first assistant Emily Charlton. After she gets hit by a taxi, second assistant Andy Sachs (Anne Hathaway) visits her hospital room. Charlton is angry and tearful at everything she is missing. “The hospital scene makes me laugh because that’s really who she is: this completely broken down, vulnerable, insecure person.”.

It has been revealed that 3. “The Young Victoria” (2010, Jean-Marc Vallée) gave Blunt a queen to embody. “I remember the scene where she asks [Prince] Albert to marry her, because he was not allowed to ask her. She is the monarch, and had to be the one to ask. That scene was so vulnerable and beautifully twinkly, how Jean-Marc shot that.”.

Sources indicate that 4. “The Adjustment Bureau,” a romantic sci-fi thriller, co-starred Matt Damon. “I remember never being able to get through a scene with Matt Damon without laughing. But I did love the scene in the bathroom where they meet. That scene had to sparkle because otherwise you don’t care about them, and you don’t care about them using their magical fedoras to get back to each other. Matt Damon doesn’t know how to be bad. That’s the truth. He doesn’t know how to play a false note. There is something about what Matt does, and he’s so dexterous in his humanity, but I don’t feel it’s technical with Matt. He’s like a laser beam of truth, and I feel myself, anyone who watches him, they ease back and they go, ‘Oh, thank God, Matt Damon’s here.’ He just leads with the truth. He’s like Josh Brolin. They only know how to be honest, and so they have such humanity to them. That’s why you can’t take your eyes off them. John [Krasinski] and I were so proud of what Matt did [with “The Odyssey”]. It’s obviously the most Herculean undertaking, but he grounded everything with that performance.”.

It has been revealed that 5. “Edge of Tomorrow” (2014, Doug Liman) co-starred Tom Cruise and thrust Blunt into action mode for the first time. Her moment was a war scene set on a beach. “It was the beach set, and we started calling it ‘the bitch’ because it was such a nightmare. That set was always flooded. You were always exposed to terrible elements of the weather, freezing, and we shot that beach scene for a month. Tom Cruise gave me a lot of flowers on that one. He was so good to me, and he revealed halfway through the shoot that this was the deep end of action for him— this was the most challenging action movie that he had ever done, and it was my first action movie, so I was flung in at the deep end of action. But we held each other through that. I loved athletics when I was a kid, and then couldn’t be bothered to work out, and then thought I knew what working out was, and then I realized I didn’t know what working out was until I started training for ‘Edge of Tomorrow,’ and that was a transformational thing to my body. She needed to look lethal, absolutely lethal. And so it helped me a lot, doing all of that physicality.”.

According to recent reports, 6. “Into the Woods” (2014, Rob Marshall), adapted from Stephen Sondheim’s stage musical, boasted a huge ensemble cast; Blunt played the baker’s wife opposite James Corden. “‘Moments in the Woods,’ that massive song she has right before she gets squished by the giant. She’s weighing up the duality of life, whether she goes for this poetic interlude in her prosaic life or if she goes back to the prosaic life. That kind of agony that she’s going through in the song was cool. I had I’d never sung in front of anyone before, really, other than one small TV thing years ago. I didn’t even want to audition for it, and Rob Marshall said, ‘Look, I’m not looking for singers who can kind of act. I’m looking for actors who can kind of sing,’ and that was great advice. I said it to my 12-year-old this morning as she went off to her musical audition at school. I said, ‘Don’t worry about the notes; just tell us a story. That’s it. That’s what the song should be, and that’s what will make it sound amazing.'”.

Industry observers note that 7. “Sicario” (2015, Denis Villeneuve) plops Blunt’s straight-arrow FBI agent into a violent Mexican border scenario. “The scene that stands out for me is a spellbinding one, when Benicio del Toro comes to my apartment, and he puts the gun to my face and forces me to sign the contract. It’s right at the end of the movie, and I think that scene holds a special place for me because we were not sure about the scene that was written by Taylor Sheridan. It didn’t feel like it belonged in what we were trying to achieve between the characters. We wanted to change it a little bit. It was an idea that Benicio had. We were racking our brains as to how to finish this scene and this moment between the two characters. He always has so many crazy ideas, and he will have some absolute bangers in there. And he called me at about 11 o’clock the night before, and he goes, ‘I think I have it. What about this?’ And I remarked, ‘That is a great idea, because you’ve got this very idealistic FBI agent who’s pulled into this incoherent, amoral world. And she’s being forced to sign a contract that says everything they did was aboveboard, and that’s like a death to a character like that.’ We rehearsed that scene for two hours. Denis loved it, and then we all turned to [cinematographer] Roger Deakins: “Roger, what do you think?” And he gave his slow nod of approval, and then we shot it, and it was so.”.

8. “A Quiet Place” (2018, John Krasinski) was Blunt’s first experience being directed by her husband. The memorable moment: giving birth in the bathtub as a killer monster hovers nearby, listening for any noise. “We shot that whole sequence from the water breaking in the bathtub in order, which I was grateful to John for. It took four days. We did two takes of that bathtub scene because he shot it mainly as a oner. It starts as the blood’s trickling out, and it comes up, and you see the creature, and then it goes into that scream, and then the fireworks go off, but yeah, it’s a wild scene. It’s really smart to have a baby in a silent world. Every woman I’ve spoken to about that scene, they go: ‘Oh my God, that scene made me cross my legs.” And I was: ‘Okay, all right.'”.

Sources indicate that 9. “Oppenheimer” (2023, Christopher Nolan) offered Blunt a constrained role as Kitty, the recessive wife of the great physicist (Cillian Murphy). Blunt agreed that the scene that earned her the Oscar nomination was in the courtroom where she is badgered by the formidable Jason Clarke. “I knew that was the monster scene. When I read the script, I thought, ‘What an extraordinary scene, that you have this person staggering in, looking like a liability,’ and Chris had written that she almost chokes, and you think she’s going to blow it. When I talked to him about it after I read the script, I mentioned, ‘What a reclamation that scene is of that extraordinary brain coming back to life.’ The brain that had gone crazy at the ironing board, probably meant for bigger things than being someone’s wife and someone’s mummy, and I had a great deal of empathy for her and a lot of women who went crazy at the ironing board. She owns Jason Clarke in a way, and you realize she could probably run circles around him. He played such a wonderful bully in that film, but we saw what Meryl [Streep] did with Miranda Priestley: There’s such power in quiet, great, great power and great dignity.”.

It has been revealed that 10. “The Devil Wears Prada 2” (2026, David Frankel) allowed Blunt to indulge Charlton’s excesses. “We all had scenery stuck in our teeth on that one. It was so fun to go back to playing that lunatic. My favorite scene was the funeral scene where she comes in and rants about Dolce and Gabbana. It was such a ludicrous outfit to be wearing to a funeral. Anne Hathaway is the most unstoppable force. And what a wide range of roles she has access to. I feel this moment in her life. She’s in this full wingspan of being able to harness everything she can do and everything she has to offer, and I can’t believe she had the year she just did, and she was pregnant!”.

Industry observers note that “Disclosure Day” (2026, Steven Spielberg) leaned on Blunt to carry the sci-fi thriller. “The four-and a-half minute oner in the beginning when she arrives at the news station. I’ve seen what Steven Spielberg can do visually, his visual prowess is rather unparalleled. So to be in a oner that he conjures up on the day, that happened spontaneously — he was planning on covering it. And I stated, ‘what would help me so much is if you could let me whirlwind out of control in one take from the moment I pull up, going into the makeup room, coming out speaking Korean, she’s in this incoherent tailspin, and then you see her disintegrate over the course of it. And she gets up there to deliver the weather, and she starts to speak in the alien language. Can we just try it as a oner, just for me to see where I’ve got to get to?’ And he watched me do it. And by the time I got up there to do the weather, my legs were shaking. I was out of breath, beside myself, and he loved it. And he goes, ‘We’re going to do it as a oner.’ And we were done by 2 pm. because he planned to shoot it all day. It was Steven in his element of going, ‘Oh, I see it’ and not only was he intentional about creating the environment for me to be able to do that so he didn’t overcover it, he saw a cinematic advantage.”.

Blunt plays several characters in one. “All the stuff in the childhood home was deeply moving because that also dealt with that moment where the character goes from crisis to serenity and the ability to then deploy these powers rather than be puppeteered by them. So I loved that shape-shift in the character, like playing two people throughout the course of this film. And the other moment that felt so human to me was the panic attack in the box car after the train sequence, and she’s at max capacity, bubbling over, overwhelmed, and a few people, including myself on set, had experienced panic attacks, and that felt like a real reaction to someone who was utterly overwhelmed. That also felt so Spielbergian: no one’s a slick elite action hero in Steven’s films. Everyone’s afraid. Everyone, including Indiana Jones, everyone’s scared. That hand that’s shaking on the way to Omaha Beach, that is trauma. He can relate to your vulnerabilities. Everyone’s a bit over their head, and in a different action movie, me and Josh O’Connor would have dropped in the boxcar and gone, ‘Whoa, that was crazy.’ And instead, she has a panic attack. I got them a lot in my early twenties, and Steven’s not immune, neither is Josh. All of us have experienced that. That moment where he takes my hands and he puts them on the piano and he goes, ‘This is real. This is real. Feel this. I’m here. You’re here. We’re here.’ I’ve done that. So it just was like, ‘Oh my God!’ You get to sublimate what you’ve experienced into this creative art form sometimes. That’s the great gift often on movies.”.

Sources indicate that the languages were right in Blunt’s wheelhouse. She has always loved languages. She learned them two to three months before the start of the shoot. “I learned those scenes. The first thing I learned was the Russian and the Korean, because I wanted it to be spoken at such a velocity that it sounded as conversational as it does as me speaking to you right now, and she doesn’t know she’s speaking Russian,” she said. “She thinks she’s speaking English. You have someone who is white-knuckling their way through most of this film, and these forms of mind control are unconscious to her in the beginning, it’s compulsive.”.

Next up: “Walk the Blue Fields” directed by John Crowley and co-starring Andrew Scott as another hot priest, Father Joe, presiding at a wedding. “It’s a short story that I bought the rights to about six years ago by Claire Keegan. If you’ve ever read any of her short stories, they’re like laser beams. They’re so wonderful. My sister Felicity is a book agent. She represents Claire, and she sent it to me. Story A is a wedding day, and story B is what led up to that wedding and why everything is starting to unravel on the wedding day. And it plays like a thriller,” she stated. “She’s coming back to Ireland to try to build a relationship with her Irish father [Ciaran Hinds] after they’ve been estranged for years, and it’s a story about identity and religion and love. Andrew Scott has to be one of the most beautiful actors I’ve ever shared a scene with.”.

And, of course, John Krasinski’s upcoming “Quiet Place 3,” which co-stars Jack O’Connell, Cillian Murphy, Jason Clarke and Noah Jupe, is shrouded in secrecy. “I don’t want to blow John’s cover here,” she remarked. And “Sicario 3” is also moving forward with the original cast, a script by James Bond writer Steven Knight and director Padraic McKinley.

Breakout star Sara Boustany is reuniting with The Body creator in an upcoming war drama movie, over a week after the Netflix show’s successful debut.

Sources indicate that the Body is Netflix's newest psychological thriller drama following a Catholic high school dance team whose Halloween initiation ritual goes terribly wrong after one of their recruits falls into a coma. Boustany portrays Elise Zakaria, one of The Body's main characters who's introduced as the unapologetic co-captain of the Lions team. The show hails from creator and showrunner Quinn Shephard, who previously directed Zoey Deutch and Dylan O'Brien in Hulu's 2022 comedy film Not Okay. Following its release, the genre-bending series became an instant social media sensation, debuting at number three on Netflix's global top ten chart in 80 countries.

Over a week after winning the hearts of audiences with her breakout performance in The Body, Boustany has officially found her first movie project as lead. According to Deadline, the Lebanese-American actor has been tapped to star in Between Us and the River, an independent coming-of-age movie set in 2005 during the Iraq War. The character-driven feature reunites her with The Body creator Quinn Shephard, who has signed on as a producer. Boustany will also be joined by fellow TV standout Amélie Hoeferle, who also recently gained recognition for her fan-favorite role in the hit Prime Video show Sterling Point.

Sources indicate that reviews for The Body praised Boustany for her sharp comedic timing and multi-layered performance as Elise. Her magnetic chemistry with co-star Kristina Bogic has also been one of the main highlights of the show. Before landing The Body, Boustany originally had minor appearances in the 2019 highlights Pen15 and Dolly Parton's Heartstrings. She also had a supporting role in 2025's Hello Beautiful movie, which featured Tricia Helfer as a famous model who gets diagnosed with breast cancer at the peak of her career.

Industry observers note that between Us and the River will center on a first-generation Iraqi-American college student and aspiring dancer, played by Boustany, who falls in love with her Mexican-American classmate. However, their relationship faces a difficult challenge when a shocking discovery leads them both to confront grief, identity, and the impact of war. Filmmaker Nika Fehmiu is directing the movie, which serves as her feature-length directorial debut. She also co-wrote the script with Baghdad Stories author Nadia Al Sultani. Before the upcoming movie, Fehmiu wrote, directed, and edited the short film Look at Me, which debuted at the Tribeca Festival.

It has been revealed that besides Boustany and Hoeferle, Between Us and the River will also star Alejandro Akara (Landman), Sarah Himadeh (The Last of Us), Laughton Royce (Clean Hands), and Sean Luc Rogers (Clarkston at Echo Theatre Company). It is produced by Shephard through her production banner, Ingénue, along with Fehmiu for North Wind Films. Nuer Taqa and Zoey Pressey of Radiance Pictures are also producing alongside Matt Cappetta of Planet 9 Films. Production on the new coming-of-age war drama movie has already been completed.

At the time of writing, the release date for Boustany's Between Us and the River movie remains under wraps.

After a dance-team initiation mishap, a group of Catholic school girls experience prophetic visions that incite mass hysteria in their town.

According to recent reports, french and Spanish sub-genres for Netflix have become associated with adrenaline-loaded flawless heists thanks to highlights like Money Heist, Lupin, and Berlin. Now another Spanish film released on October 30 is breaking charts and making a name for itself. According to Nielsen, the film has been able to accumulate 162 million watched-minutes on U.S. televisions during November 2–8, enough to make it the #10 streaming movie in America that week. The Spanish heist thriller is set in Madrid during the 2013 financial crisis, where a quartet of thieves pulls off a bank heist, only for a sudden getaway car crash to fracture the timeline and expose deep betrayals among the crew.

While the film is strictly a crime thriller, it has a “what-if” structure to show different perspectives and post-car-crash outcomes, which help it carry a nice looping structure. The title of the film is Collision Course, and according to Netflix’s official global Top 10 data, the 106-minute Spanish thriller has accumulated 31.6 million views across its first three chart weeks. The timing of the release made a perfect collision course for fans of Lupin too, who probably watched Lupin Season 4 through October 23 and onward, only to find that same energy in Collision Course when it was released on November 30.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

Sources indicate that collision Course, officially titled Colisión in Spanish, is structurally closer to Run Lola Run or Krzysztof Kieślowski's Blind Chance than a straightforward bank-heist movie. It demonstrates a time loop that progressively gives the heist more nuance as a variation reveals another relationship, secret, or motivation until viewers understand considerably more than any individual character does. A different layer of deception gets revealed each time. This doesn’t necessarily make it sci-fi because it’s vastly different from what a movie like Palm Springs does.

Recent findings suggest that however, while this unique structure has allowed Collision Course to chart globally and specifically in the U.S., it hasn’t necessarily given its Rotten Tomatoes ratings the same come-up. There are very few reviews on RT at the time of writing, so there’s no exact score there, but the film has managed to rake in 5.6/10 ratings on IMDB from roughly 2k reviewers.

There's another fun bit of context. During the same November 2–8 Netflix reporting week in which Collision Course became the #1 non-English movie with 17.2 million views, Lupin Part 4 remained #3 among non-English TV with 6.1 million views and 36.6 million hours watched. Earlier Lupin parts were simultaneously charting again too. So the simultaneous European heist releases have clearly helped Netflix synergize greatly.

The DXRacer Martian Pro offers massaging, heating, cooling and electronic adjustment. It’s sturdy and also fairly comfortable for a gaming chair. Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Recent findings suggest that if you want a gaming chair that tries to do literally everything, allow me to introduce you to the DXRacer Martian Pro. It’ll massage you, heat your butt, and even cool your you-know-whats thanks to a built-in fan (which I’ve affectionately labelled “the junk wafter”).

It has adjustable lumbar support, adjustable arm rests, an adjustable head rest, and loads of control over positioning thanks to its electronic controls. It’s built well and moderately comfortable… for a gaming chair (spoiler: that’s foreshadowing).

Recent findings suggest that however, despite its many positives, the chair isn’t perfect. It’s very expensive at $899, and obviously all those goodies up there need juice, which means cables. It’s also a gaming chair, meaning it’s about as comfortable as most gaming chairs — so not very.

But could this still be the best gaming chair for you? Find out in my full DXRacer Martian Pro review.

The Martian Pro packs lots of features, plenty of adjustment and a heavy, sturdy design. It’s also fairly comfortable as far as gaming chairs go.

Sources indicate that the best thing about the Martian Pro is its wide array of cool features. Unlike the base DXRacer Martian, the Pro has a built-in back massager, like those chairs at airports. There are loads of different modes, and the massaging is genuinely pretty good. I found myself oof-ing on quite a few occasions as the massage balls dug into tight spots on my back. The massage only lasts for 10 minutes if you don’t press the cycle button, so you have to either cycle through constantly or restart regularly. This is a little annoying, but not a huge deal — I’d rather it turned itself off than keep running — and you’ll rapidly get used to where your favorite massage setting is in the cycle order. I like massage setting two, which made things fairly easy.

The base of the chair has a heating element, so you can warm up your butt during colder seasons. But there’s also a cooling fan for when your junk gets a little hot. As I mentioned up top, I’ve christened it “the junk wafter”. It really works, providing a strong cooling breeze. Now, given not everyone is as hygienic as I am (and I’m sure you are, dear reader), I can think of obvious downsides related to blowing air up and over the ol’ undercarriage. But hey, as long as you’re on your own at your gaming desk, who am I to judge you for cooling down your best bits?

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

It has been revealed that you can’t heat, cool or massage without electricity, so it figures that DXRacer gave the Martian Pro electronic adjustment. The chair back is adjusted using a toggle on the left base, while the two-part lumbar pad is adjusted on the right.

Un-electronically, there’s a seat height paddle, and four-axis armrests that offer an impressive amount of adjustment (and can have their tops replaced when worn out). This lets you fine tune the chair’s shape and support.

In a recent development, the DXRacer Martian Pro is built pretty well. I’m not so keen on all the red accents, as I think they look a little childish and more than a little tacky, so initially I had my doubts about whether the chair would feel sturdy. But it does, for the most part.

Industry observers note that as soon as you try and get this behemoth out the box, you’ll notice it’s extremely large and very heavy, which is reassuring. The leather feels premium, there’s nice spongy padding on the armrests, and all the buttons and electronics work as they should. It never feels like it’s going to break on you.

According to recent reports, my only gripe is that the plastic side trims that cover the pivot mechanism look cheap and feel all scratchy, as a result of cheap plastic. On a nearly-$900 chair, I’d expect better.

Now, there’s a monumental caveat here: I’ll cover it in more detail later on, but in short, gaming chairs are all about show — they almost all use an inherently uncomfortable flat-backed design.

That remarked, as gaming chairs go, this one is alright. That’s primarily thanks to the adjustable lumbar pad, which provides support for your back. It’s nowhere near as substantial, pronounced and supportive as the large (necessarily so) lumbar supports on the best office chairs, but better than nothing — i.e. better than the Razer Soma Chroma I tested recently. There’s also lots of padding on the arm rests and an included neck cushion (although I found this a little too large).

If you want a gaming chair that’s as comfortable as they come, check out the Razer Iskur V2 NewGen, which has a much larger lumbar pad and a decidedly ergonomic design.

It has been revealed that alas, if you want proper support and comfort, this chair isn’t for you. It needs to be charged regularly and is quite complicated to build. And there’s no way I’d recommend paying $900.

Recent findings suggest that as I mentioned above, gaming chairs are almost all inherently uncomfortable. Flat backs and necks, padded rather than mesh bases, small lumbar cushions, etc. This makes their very existence weird and kinda meta: they only exist because streamers and YouTubers use them (as they look "gamer-y), which makes the general public want them too. Certain brands therefore supply the aforementioned streamers and influencers with them, which keeps the public buying them. Ah, the circle of modern life.

Sources indicate that what I’m trying to say here is, if you want a comfortable time, do not get a gaming chair. There’s absolutely no reason why you can’t game in a luxurious office chair, and if you ask me, that’s what you should do. For the same or less money, you can get a much more comfortable and supportive chair. It's just that you won't look like a streamer.

The Martian Pro has lumbar support, yes, but even at its greatest extent it’s just a small mound. The Boulies EP460, Boulies EP500, Autonomous ErgoChair Pro and Sihoo Doro C300 Pro V2 all have huge mesh lumbar pads, which is what you actually need to properly support your back.

Industry observers note that I found the Martian Pro’s neck cushion ridiculously oversized, and extremely firm, meaning no give. The result was that my head and neck were pushed forward — as if I were doing Jim Carrey’s trademark bird-like head thrust.

It has been revealed that worst of all is the seat pad. I have a type of immuno-arthritis that affects my legs and lower back, so it’s important my seat pads are comfortable. Let me tell you now: there is nothing quite like mesh for butt and coccyx comfort (and natural cooling as a secondary benefit). The Martian Pro uses a basic cushion, which is fairly thick, but still puts too much compression on my lower back. I had to use a coccyx cushion to stay comfortable.

According to recent reports, as I already mentioned, all those electronics above need power, which means the Martian Pro needs a cable. Now, to its credit, there’s a battery inside (and a fairly significant 5,000mAh one at that). After a full charge, the chair lasted me a few hours of massaging while gaming.

You need to charge it regularly, though, which I found annoying. What’s worse is that when you’ve run out of charge, you can’t adjust the recline or lumbar support as both are done electronically.

It’s just too complicated for me. Again, I’d prefer the natural cooling and better analog lumbar support of a decent mesh office chair.

According to recent reports, thanks to all those electronics, the Martian Pro is somewhat tricky to build. While each step is fairly easy, there are just lots of them and the chair is extremely heavy — I’d recommend having two people and a lot of space before building it. You’ve also got to make sure everything is wired in properly, which can be a little confusing. I didn’t quite hide one wire properly so had to backtrack and redo my steps at one point.

The Martian Pro took me 42 minutes to build alone, and I was drenched in sweat afterwards. I’ve built a lot of chairs in my time as reviews editor here at Tom’s Guide, so I’m an experienced builder — I once put together the Boulies OP180 in just 10 minutes! 42 minutes is a long time for me.

In a recent development, there’s absolutely no way on Earth this chair should cost $899 / £649. Sure, it has some nifty features and is built well, but it looks pretty cheap and tacky with the red accents — it’s like a five-year-old’s fever dream. To be fair, you can buy it in a plain black model, which I’d recommend. But as I mentioned above, some of the plastics used are scratchy and cheap, too.

If you want to look like your favorite streamer, and be just as uncomfortable, you can pick up the SecretLab Titan Evo for $569, which looks much more premium. Even the Razer Iskur V2 NewGen — the gold standard of gaming chairs from a comfort perspective — costs only $649 from latest, which pretty well puts things into perspective: the Martian Pro is overpriced.

Recent findings suggest that the DXRacer Martian Pro is unfortunately a mixed bag. It packs lots of features and is fairly comfortable for a gaming chair. It offers lots of adjustment and a sturdy build. But I can’t give this chair one of our higher scores and my outright recommendation. It’s not truly comfortable in the same way as an office chair. It’s complicated to build and needs a cable to function, and for $900 I’d expect near perfection, not to mention a premium-looking design. Maybe this one’s better suited for Mars.

He pointed out that when Baby Mac gets kidnapped by a murder of crows under the command of the dread sorceress Alexandra (Carey Mulligan), the amount of work to achieve that moment fully through stop-motion would mean they’d probably still be animating it. Related Stories From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments How Sound Design Helps ‘Minotaur’ Get Away with Murder.

Sources indicate that “We’ll often get [animators] to produce some practical work to lead the visual effects work. We built a crow puppet to spec. We didn’t animate it in the film, but it informed the visual effects work. We try to stay away from simulations as much as possible, knowing that what we’re chasing is something that feels handmade and something that is slightly imperfect,” Dubuc stated.

It has been revealed that that goes for individual characters and for the vibrant backgrounds of “Wildwood” alike. “The audience would think that we built sets the size of an airport hangar with a hundred thousand practical puppets running downhill. It’s not possible,” Dubuc remarked. The fact that it looks possible, in both the most intricate battle sequences and the ordinary chaos of biking past Powell’s Books, means that the VFX team has done its job. “ The portrayal of Portland that we were striving for is a beautiful, vibrant city,” Dubuc said.

Breaking: AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (971 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Indiewire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.
  • As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.
  • But the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were confirmed Monday, November 23.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” an upcoming film from YouTuber Gossip Goblin that was made entirely with generated artificial intelligence, was deemed ineligible for the Best Animated Feature Oscar at the upcoming Academy Awards.

As IndieWire previously reported on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” which is the first fully AI movie to be released theatrically, the film had submitted for consideration and had planned FYC screenings alongside its theatrical release on December 4.

But the film was not included among the list of 38 animated films deemed eligible for this year’s Oscars that were confirmed Monday, November 23. IndieWire understands that the Academy’s Animation Branch Executive Committee determined “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not meet the Academy’s definition of an animated film under the rules for the 99th Awards. Related Stories The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch From ‘Disclosure Day’ to ‘Devil Wears Prada’: Emily Blunt Breaks Down 10 of Her Greatest Movie Moments.

Here’s the full rule as written that the Academy felt “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” did not satisfy:.

It has been revealed that an animated film is one in which characters or objects are given the illusion of life by having movement created for them, by any human means. While the crucial movement of a live-action motion picture is captured at speed, animation is the craft of human creation and manipulation of images to produce a performance from inanimate objects. At least 75 percent of the motion picture’s running time, without opening or end credits, must include animation of the primary subject or subjects. An animated feature has a running time of more than 40 minutes. Upon submission, filmmakers must provide information supporting how the motion picture qualifies as an animated film.

Industry observers note that edward Saatchi, a producer on “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” with Fable Studios, told IndieWire he and director Zack London (a.k.a. Gossip Goblin) initiative to appeal the animation branch’s decision and cited the example of Richard Linklater’s rotoscoped film “Apollo 10 1/2,” which was originally deemed ineligible but saw the branch reverse its decision upon appeal. Saatchi remarked that the film, in addition to submitting for Best Animated Feature, also submitted in other categories such as Best Director, Adapted Screenplay, VFX, and Sound. But if the film doesn’t fall under the animation branch today, he believes eventually AI movies will inevitably find a place somewhere within Academy rules, even if it ends up being a theoretical “Best AI Movie” category.

“‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ is starting a massive debate around where cinematic works of art made with AI fit. Is it time to consider a ‘Best AI Movie?’ Do these films fit best in the voice-actor led animation category? Is AI simply the new VFX? It’s going to take the whole industry time to figure it out,” Saatchi remarked. “With traditional garlanded directors like Matthieu Kassovitz, Alex Proyas, and Doug Liman making heavily-AI films, it’s going to be a good debate of how to categorize. We think Best Animated is simplest, but it may be the Academy decides ultimately that a Best AI movie category will make the most sense with these films where everything you’re seeing is generative.”.

Of note, one of the films that did qualify for Best Animated Feature was “Coyote vs. Acme,” which is a hybrid animated and live-action film featuring the Looney Tunes alongside human actors in the real world. The Academy on Monday also revealed the eligible features in the Best Documentary Feature race and the Best International Feature race.

As part of the Academy’s most recent rules changes from earlier this year, only roles credited in the film’s legal billing that are demonstrably performed by humans with their consent are eligible for acting categories, and screenplays must be human-authored to be eligible. That rule changed followed on guidelines from last year ahead of the 98th Oscars in which the Academy specified, “[Gen-AI] tools neither help nor harm the chances of achieving a nomination. The Academy and each branch will judge the achievement, taking into account the degree to which a human was at the heart of the creative authorship when choosing which movie to award.”.

In the case of “Gods Don’t Give Gifts,” the film has a script written by London, and though all the characters in the film are generated with AI visually, it features real human actors doing the voice work for the characters. The film also features cameos of some real-life people playing parts resembling themselves, most notably the pop star Grimes. But the film has elaborate look books, visual reference points, and photo mashing that all went into the creation of these characters, something that clearly has human authorship and goes beyond a computer interpreting a single prompt.

According to recent reports, part of Gossip Goblin’s battle in legitimizing “Gods Don’t Give Gifts” is in showing there was a human team, between 30-35 people, working for years on the film’s creation. Gossip Goblin also recently released a behind-the-scenes documentary that showcases the film’s composer, its foley artist, its voice actors, and more detailing the human effort that went into the project.

Discussion over AI in Oscar eligible films came to a head after several movies in the 2024 Oscar race were reported to have included AI in their post-production editing process, including “A Complete Unknown,” “The Brutalist,” and “Emilia Pérez.” The examples were for traditional VFX, not for anything that enhanced or altered performances, but the Academy as a result now requires disclosure of AI if it is used in a film.

“Gods Don’t Give Gifts” begins its theatrical run on December 4, which will initially be an Oscar-qualifying run, and it will expand on January 22 alongside a rollout with the film’s international distributor AGC International.

Additional reporting by Marcus Jones.

Amanda M. Castro is a Network TV writer at Collider and a Fresh York–based journalist whose work has appeared in Newsweek, where she is an Associate Editor, and The U.S. Sun, where she previously served as a Senior Consumer Reporter.

She specializes in network television coverage, delivering sharp, thoughtful analysis of long-running procedural hits and ambitious new dramas across broadcast TV. At Collider, Amanda explores character arcs, storytelling trends, and the cultural impact of network series that keep audiences tuning in week after week.

Born and raised in Puerto Rico, Amanda is bilingual and holds a degree in Communication, Film, and Media Studies from the University of New Haven.

It has been revealed that tony Soprano (James Gandolfini) is adept at making heartrending situations seem like unavoidable consequences of fate. This is one of his strengths whenever he sits in Dr. Jennifer Melfi's (Lorraine Bracco) office, where even a moment of clarity can become an opportunity to justify himself. In Season 1, Episode 7, "Down Neck," Tony gives one of his most revealing remarks about his character: "You're born into this s**t; you are what you are.".

He’s discussing his father, Johnny Boy Soprano (Joseph Siravo), and the childhood that led him down the path of organized crime, almost like a family lineage. Beyond the fact that the discussion matters, he’s not just telling his childhood story. He’s in therapy because of his son, A.J. Melfi (Robert Iler) wants to know what Tony was like at his son’s age. In trying to explain his son, he starts telling stories from his own life.

It’s a fascinating choice; he understands that his childhood was shaped by things he couldn’t control. What he finds hard to understand is that A.J. is raised in a completely different environment, where Tony is already a father. The quotation suggests Tony is willing to make peace with his past, but it also shows he doesn’t consider major changes in the future.

It has been revealed that tony's recollections of his father are complicated, but Johnny Boy's impact is undeniable. He was a gangster whose line of work involved violence and intimidation, and Tony witnessed this world closely. He remembers the more pleasant details: his father's fondness for food, his enjoyment of life, and his fondness for people. Tony's memories of his father go beyond seeing him as the one-dimensional gangster. He also remembers his father, whom he respected, noting that what made him admirable at one point was also what made him dangerous.

On the other hand, his mother, Livia (Nancy Marchand), certainly didn't provide comfort and support. Tony's connection to her was also strained, and he often struggles to remember his childhood. Besides punishment and problems, the family indicated little warmth, unlike his father's, so it's understandable that Tony sees his life as shaped by circumstances and events in his early life, long before he could understand them.

Recent findings suggest that the interesting point, though, is that Tony had some other options. He was bright and sporty enough to pursue a different path in life and his dreams outside the underworld and his father's operation. His view of himself, portraying himself as simply being who he is supposed to be, seems to be unrealistic.

It has been revealed that the ironic twist in "Down Neck" is that, although Tony recounts his childhood, he does so because of A.J.'s concerns. He thinks A.J. would join the Mafia like him, but Tony realizes A.J. is a softer child who might not be cut out for the life Tony is living.

Recent findings suggest that despite his good intentions, Tony's understanding of protection is rather twisted. Meadow (Jamie-Lynn Sigler) and A.J. enjoy the luxury that comes with Tony's criminal profession. Tony believes he can give Meadow and A.J. everything that comes with his criminal career without exposing them to its sources of wealth. In other words, he thinks that he can protect and be generous at the same time while restricting the flow of information about his true life. Tony lies and deceives his kids, preparing them to accept the good things in life as well-deserved.

A.J. is especially interesting in this case because Tony worries that his son has inherited some of his personal struggles, but he pays little attention to his parenting. A child doesn't need to inherit bad qualities to pick up bad habits by watching his parents; Tony worries about A.J.'s future but doesn't set a good example of the path he wants his kid to avoid.

It has been revealed that one reason the show remains interesting is that it takes the protagonist's mind seriously. The sessions with the therapist are a place for Tony to talk about anything he has on his mind, including his childhood, panic attacks, different reluctant feelings, and the things that still haunt him as an adult. For a time, the audience believes Tony may solve his problems through therapy; however, Melfi comes to a different conclusion. In the penultimate episode of the show, “The Blue Comet,” the therapist decides to end their relationship when she gets to know that sociopaths often use therapy to achieve their goals. This suggests that the audience has paid close attention to the sessions where the protagonist discusses issues he may do nothing about.

In a recent development, at that moment, the difference between understanding oneself and wishing for improvement is clear. For several years, Tony has talked about his father, mother, and many other influences on his life. After talking about his past, he can make sense of his actions and attitudes, but that doesn’t mean he wants to take responsibility. The most annoying thing about Tony is that he doesn't completely disregard the outcome of his actions; he has enough information to feel concerned about his children’s future and understands he wouldn't want his children to grow up the way he did. Still, again and again, he tries to justify his behavior by arguing that it is simply his nature.

Nineteen years after the last episode of The Sopranos, that line still hurts because it sounds like a valid thought. It isn't valid, though; it is just another excuse to avoid a difficult conversation. Johnny Boy shaped Tony Soprano, but Tony has had enough time to make his own choices. His children have to pay for those choices and actions.

There’s a storm brewing, chere, and it has nothing to do with the weird Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Herbie the Robot Dunkin Donuts ads that played like once a quarter during all the football games on Sunday.

The final trailer was released ahead of Marvel’s “Avengers: Doomsday,” the mega-Sentinel, crossover-tastic 165-minute Russo Brothers opus out on December 18. And the response hasn’t been great — in part because Cyclops says, “To me, my X-Men!” and there isn’t actually a Storm.

Way back in the salad days of 2012, Joss Whedon first did an “Assemble” shot that roved in a circle all of the original “Avengers” film, while an Alan Silvestri score bwaaamped the brassy “Avengers” theme. Say whatever you like about Whedon’s strengths and weaknesses when it comes to visual style, but the first time this happened, the shot’s continuous nature served a storytelling purpose. It was the cinematic way to finally bind these crazy kids together in superhero fellowship — through the timeless crucible of Newly introduced York City getting shredded into CGI bits by alien-monster things. Related Stories AI Film ‘Gods Don’t Give Gifts’ Deemed Ineligible by Academy for Best Animated Feature Oscar The Best Visual Effects in ‘Wildwood’ Are the Ones You Can’t See — Watch.

Recent findings suggest that but over the many, many Phases of the MCU, the Avengers Assemble shots have kept happening. And happening. And sure enough, the “Doomsday” trailer crescendos with a bunch of our heroes stuck in a gray-black wasteland void that looks like a glitched “Expedition 33” loading screen, with the camera straining to create that same sense of unity.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t. At least not in the trailer. Which is why so much of the response to the finale “Doomsday” trailer has been focused on it.

According to recent reports, as folks online have pointed out, Steve Rogers (Chris Evans) looks like he’s standing in entirely different lighting from the people closest to him. There’s no sense of texture or proximity that suggests anybody was placed against the same green screen together, let alone acting together (a problem that has been pointed out about the filmmaking process for “Doomsday” already).

According to recent reports, no amount of money can make up for shooting for maximum flexibility — which so often can devolve into being indecisive — or for pursuing relentless revisions throughout the VFX pipeline. That is exactly what leads to shadowy, sloppily-framed environments like wherever the hell the Avengers are fighting Doctor Doom (Robert Downey Jr.) and his creations. And because the environment is so flattened and indistinct, only the barest hints of color survive. And really, only because Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal) is still wearing a coat from a different movie.

According to recent reports, now, what comes most naturally to Cyclops is shooting an optic blast from his eyes, and what comes most naturally to us is posting negative takes online. The trailer takes that shot out of context for nostalgia’s sake; its dramatic purpose within the film itself might be more complicated, or the setup for a twist in three different timelines’ worth of Avengers’ fortunes. But when it comes to all the cinematic crimes of artless visuals, repetitive plots, and overbearing lore that have contributed to superhero fatigue? The “Avengers: Doomsday” trailer doesn’t seem to be beating the charges.

Tech Report: 7 Best Gangsters From Guy Ritchie Highlights

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team.
  • It has been revealed that from improbably named and larger than life characters like Lock, Stock, and Two Smoking Barrels' Hatchet Harry and Snatch's Bullet Tooth Tony, to the genuinely terrifying, like Mobland's Harry Da Souza, nobody writes gangster characters like Guy Ritchie.
  • The TV shows based on Guy Ritchie's movies have had mixed success as not all of them have got the formula and tone right.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that faith Roswell is a Senior Writer on Screen Rant's Classic TV team. Since earning her degree in Creative Writing over a decade ago, Faith has written articles on film and TV from a variety of different angles. Faith now combines her knowledge of psychology with her love of monster movies to give more insight into what makes the best ones. You may have read her Screen Rant lists and features covering horror, sci-fi, and fantasy, or read her Amazon Top 10 book, "Movie Monsters of the Deep." Faith has had an extensive career as a writer, appearing on BBC live radio, researching true crime for Rotten Mango podcast, and writing for publications including Mental Floss, Atlas Obscura, and The Daily Jaws before beginning here at Screen Rant.

It has been revealed that from improbably named and larger than life characters like Lock, Stock, and Two Smoking Barrels' Hatchet Harry and Snatch's Bullet Tooth Tony, to the genuinely terrifying, like Mobland's Harry Da Souza, nobody writes gangster characters like Guy Ritchie. The iconic director made his career writing gritty but cinematic crime comedies with twisting plots that interconnect in a way that has been emulated ever since, with many of the best crime TV shows of all time being influenced by his signature style.

The TV shows based on Guy Ritchie's movies have had mixed success as not all of them have got the formula and tone right. However, this changed with The Gentlemen, loosely connected to his movie of the same name, which perfectly nailed the combination of brutality and hilarity. Followed up by MobLand, Guy Ritchie's TV shows are now going from strength to strength, with some of his best TV gangster characters set to become as notorious as any in his movies.

Industry observers note that while his dramatization of a real-life robbery in The Diamond Heist introduced us to Lee Wenham and his story, and Lock, Stock... continued his tradition of chaotic but memorable characters like Miami Vice, Three Feet, and Firebug, MobLand and The Gentlemen have given us some of the best gangster characters in TV history.

In a recent development, helen Mirren is one of the greatest actors working today, and while she is best known for iconic roles like Queen Elizabeth and emotionally complex comedy dramas, like Calendar Girls, she has played her fair share of gangster and crime-adjacent characters too, like Queenie in Hobbs and Shaw, and Victoria in The Long Good Friday. Still, none beat Maeve Harrigan in MobLand. The Harrigans are one of TV's best crime families, and Maeve proves that a character does not need to be physically intimidating or loud in order to be utterly terrifying.

She is every bit as dangerous as the men surrounding her, understanding the underlying structure behind their empire perhaps better than any of them. Unlike most gangster families, like the Sopranos and the Sons of Anarchy MC, Maeve routinely betrays her family, proving that a great gangster character does not have to be likable. Maeve is a manipulative wildcard willing to trade everything she has for power and control, which makes her one of the most unpredictable and unusual of Guy Ritchie's characters, and all the more fascinating for it.

According to recent reports, guy Ritchie's projects are extremely British, using East End settings, distinctive dialects, and signature British humor. In a great role reversal for the many gangster movies and TV highlights set in the US, it is the American character who stands out in the chaos of The Gentlemen. Uncle Stan is a calculating and seemingly cold-blooded strategist whose methamphetamine empire is his life's work. Played by Giancarlo Esposito, this might sound uncannily like his career-making Breaking Bad character, Gus Fring. However, the two only share basic similarities, and Uncle Stan fits right into Ritchie's world while Fring would not.

Uncle Stan is fascinated by British aristocracy, which is reflected in his stylish appearance and demeanor. His monologue on British tailoring reveals how desperate he is to become part of what he sees as the elite, while his commentary contrasting the criminal underworld with privileged society is the best line in The Gentlemen and defines the show in just a few words. Esposito was the perfect casting choice for the character, as he is able to convey menace through stillness and a glance, while the character gives him more to play with through his eccentricity.

According to recent reports, the Bible-quoting gangster might not have lasted for long in The Gentlemen, but he stole every scene he had, using scripture to justify his every criminal action and leading prayers before a raid. Ritchie's ability to create a fully rounded character through just a few details is on display here, with John's organ music ringtone playing "Heaven is a Place on Earth," and his crucifixion-like posture as he rides with a gun in his hand.

Many of Ritchie's characters are walking contradictions, often being animal lovers but perfectly willing to torture human characters, or hardened criminals who appear entirely different when in the same room as their mothers. This contrast applies to virtually all of the characters in The Gentlemen, and yet Gospel John still stands out, which is a testament to Ritchie's writing and Pearce Quigley's performance. John is ridiculous, but no less dangerous, and even his violent ending did not overshadow his best scenes in the show.

According to recent reports, most of Ritchie's movies and TV shows have been male-centered, with few notable female characters. This has changed dramatically in recent years, with Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario) not only being one of The Gentlemen's best characters, but one of the most compelling female gangsters on TV. Susie Glass improves one major character from the original The Gentlemen movie, despite the two projects telling standalone stories, highlighting how Ritchie is evolving as a writer and director. The daughter of criminal patriarch Bobby Glass, she keeps the operation running as the unshakable logistics co-ordinator.

The Gentlemen has been renewed for a third season.

Rather than remaining behind the scenes, managing the business dealings on paper, Susie is an integral part of the criminal empire and her working relationship with Eddie Horniman regularly proves her expertise. Even in the moments that see her sitting quietly to the side, she is the show's reigning authority, even at the center of some of the most ludicrous scenes, including keeping a straight face during the infamous "chicken suit" moment.

Even after a long career playing tough men and criminal enforcers, MobLand's Harry Da Souza is easily one of Tom Hardy's greatest gangster characters. As the Harrigan family's trusted fixer, Da Souza has an interesting position in their world. While not an official part of the family, he is utterly loyal to them, rejecting bribes and proving himself capable of virtually anything while protecting their safety. Unlike other characters with similar roles, he is calm, measured, and patient, with the confrontation in episode 2's smoky club showing his skills at their best.

From Max Rockatansky to Ronnie Kray, Tom Hardy can bring quiet characters to life in a way few other actors can, and this makes Da Souza one of the best in MobLand. Others characters listen when he speaks, while the viewer sees the emotional layer under the surface, with his line to Conrad, "it's all war," acknowledging his acceptance of his own life, without normalizing it. Even so, rather than turning Da Souza into a "reluctant gangster with a heart" cliché, his showdown with Valjon and the concrete reminds us of the violence he is capable of.

The Gentlemen added 33 million viewing hours to streaming charts, dominating the crime TV landscape and bringing Guy Ritchie's signature style to TV in a way that had been attempted but was never truly successful. This feat was largely due to the show's characters, who represent the best of Ritchie, being eccentric, dangerous, and rarely predictable. Bobby Glass (Ray Winstone) represents the old school criminal empire, tricking even his allies through loyalty tests and pulling strings even from behind bars.

Recent findings suggest that one of the best and funniest aspects of Bobby is the way he treats his criminal dealings as a normal business, apparently considering himself respectable and competent, while his work just happens to contain a lot of illegal activity. This is absurd but it gives the character a confidence that is hard to shake. Whether at the estate or in prison, Bobby never needs to demonstrate his authority as everyone recognizes it when he enters the room.

MobLand introduced Guy Ritchie's best villain in season 2, with Frankie "The Beast" Cooper (Johnny Flynn) instantly making his mark on the show and characters. He is wildly unpredictable, sometimes cartoonish, and utterly unhinged. We see Frankie barbecuing in a Hawaiian shirt, getting a pedicure, and brutally murdering pets, yet he is eerily competent, making him one of the most disturbing characters Guy Ritchie has ever sent to the screen.

From the tracksuit to the haircut and demeanor, Frankie has more in common with the terrifying Jimmies from the apocalyptic 28 Days Later franchise than most other TV gangsters, but this is what makes him such an excellent character. He does not conform to the image of a typical British crime boss, a bloodthirsty enforcer, or one of Ritchie's hilariously incompetent small-time criminal characters that would often appear in this way. Instead, he is something else entirely, and if he appears in the upcoming third season, he is certain to steal the show.

📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 9to5mac ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (823 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions.
  • While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”.

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”.

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:.

Sources indicate that in fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In his long-spanning career, Nicolas Cage has given us numerous amazing movies across various genres, including Western, drama, comedy, and superhero. The actor keeps his audience engaged by consistently delivering a range of diverse characters, be it a fictionalized version of himself in The Unbearable Weight of Massive Talent; playing a down-on-his-luck superhero, Ben Riley, in Spider-Noir; a toxic boss who also happens to be Dracula in Renfield; or playing the titular character in David O. Russell’s biographical drama Madden, his latest film.

It has been revealed that one of his most iconic roles in recent years is the titular serial killer in Osgood Perkins' Longlegs. The 2024 psychological horror-mystery, written and directed by Perkins, is among the most eerie and borderline disturbing features in the past decade. The film follows FBI Agent Lee Harker (Maika Monroe), who is assigned to an unsolved serial killer case that takes an unexpected turn, revealing evidence of the occult. Things take a darker turn when Harker discovers a personal connection to the killer and now must stop him before he strikes again.

It has been revealed that perkins created an unsettling atmosphere not by traditional jump scares, but through sensory manipulation, framing, and uncanny character design. The vast empty spaces in frames let fans check every shadow in the corner for dread. Cinematographer Andres Arochi uses muted grays, washed-out browns, and harsh winter lighting to strip away any sense of comfort. Cage played the character with an eerie feel under heavy pale prosthetics, a ragged blonde wig, and vocally gave Longlegs an erratic shift from whispers to screams to make him more unpredictable. The marketing of the film kept his evil avatar under wraps, so fans were scared firsthand in theatres.

The film proved a commercial success, earning approximately $128 million worldwide on a $10 million budget. It further earned critical acclaim, garnering an 85% Rotten Tomatoes rating, with critics who collectively agreed, “Saturated in disquieting mood while leveraging a nightmarishly gonzo performance by Nicolas Cage, Longlegs is a satanic horror that effectively instills panic.” Fans who’d love to check out the feature or revisit it are in luck as Longlegs is making its way to Netflix this December, as per ComicBook. The film also features some compelling performances from Monroe as Lee Harker, Alicia Witt as her religious mother, Ruth Harker, Kiernan Shipka as Carrie Anne, among others.

It has been revealed that check out Longlegs on Netflix starting December 10. Stay tuned to Collider for more such updates.

Rumors about next year’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models have been ramping up, and they suggest Apple is designing an ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ that combines traits from two current models.

Apple keeps expanding the iPhone line to include newly introduced models. And while it’s great that there are more models for differing preferences and needs, it’s also left me missing the days of having one model that was the clear “best.”.

That problem isn’t going away, since the iPhone Duo represents a brand new type of iPhone that some users will love, while others find it isn’t for them.

Industry observers note that with my failed iPhone Duo experiment over, I’m back to using iPhone 18 Pro as my default model. But I still have an iPhone Air around for work, and every time I pick it up, I’m struck by how impressive it remains.

Industry observers note that I used the iPhone Air all of last year and loved it. The main reason I upgraded to an iPhone 18 Pro is the camera system. I have young children at home—including newborn twins—and want to capture the best possible photos before they get older.

iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera has been fantastic, and it’s great having the Telephoto again too.

But I still sorely miss the overall design of the iPhone Air. And it sounds like next year, I could get the best of both models.

Rumors indicate Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone Pro models will have a unique newly introduced design featuring a quad-curved display that makes it look bezel-free.

According to recent reports, the new models are expected to also be a bit slimmer, use curved edges, and possibly even bring back titanium. Leakers say the new design borrows a lot from the iPhone Air’s look.

This sounds like exactly what I’ve been hoping for.

It has been revealed that if they make one the size of the iPhone 13 mini I will buy. Otherwise I'm holding out.

While the ‘iPhone 20 Pro’ certainly won’t—and shouldn’t—be as thin as iPhone Air, if it can slim down a little and adopt several other Air design traits, I suspect it will evoke the same affection the Air has.

But unlike the Air, the new Pro model will still offer the best camera system in an iPhone (not to mention better battery life).

As a huge fan of the design of the Air, and the functionality of the 18 Pro, Apple’s 20th anniversary iPhone model could prove the perfect model for me. And for anyone else not opting for iPhone Duo 2.

It has been revealed that adaptiLift Chassis 3.0 enables the Saros 20 to move freely around the most largest and most complex of homes. A combination of an advanced vision system, adaptive algorithms, and a mechanical system comprising a main wheel, auxiliary wheel, and climbing arm mean that the device can cope with most thresholds between rooms. This even includes double layer thresholds, totaling 3.46 inches.

Industry observers note that the Saros 20 uses StarSight Autonomous System 2.0, an industry-first navigation system with true 3D mapping of your home. The setup combines LiDAR with time-of-flight measurements to create an accurate depth map with both visual and infrared camera systems. The specs are unrivaled, with a sampling frequency more than 20 times higher than other devices and 21,600 sensor points, but what counts are the results. The AI powered system can recognize more than 300+ types of obstacles, even when they are are less than an inch in width and height. That means it can avoid anything from a loose cable to an inquisitive pet.

AdaptiLift technology combines with a Carpet Intelligence System to enables the Saros 20 to detect when it is moving from solid flooring to carpet. At the most basic level, this means the mops will never get your carpets wet, but the system is far more sophisticated than this. The robot will automatically lift itself up onto deep pile carpets before lowering to the optimal height for vacuuming. It can cope with carpets with a pile height of 1.18 inches.

Finally, Smart Proposal 3.0 is the AI-powered intelligent cleaning system that analyzes your home’s unique layout, floor materials, and the behavior patterns of everyone in the home in order to automatically optimise its cleaning routines. You also get voice and app control and can even check on your pets while away by asking the Saros 20 to locate them and provide a live video feed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Editor’s Note: The following contains spoilers for The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins Season 2, Episode 4.

It has been revealed that for Reggie Dinkins (Tracy Morgan), Thanksgiving is about family, food, and making sure no one ever scores more than seven touchdowns during the big game. So when his record is on the line in Season 2 of The Fall and Rise of Reggie Dinkins, Rusty (Bobby Moynihan) uses his “One Wish Willow” to make the guy about to break it… explode. While he should’ve been more specific, things don’t go as planned.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, Brina (Precious Way) is trying to get through dinner without getting on the wrong side of Reggie’s mom, Gigi (Leslie Uggams). But right when Jerry Basmati (Craig Robinson) celebrates the upcoming record, everybody finds out the big secret: Carmelo and Jerry’s daughter Delilah (Arica Himmel) are dating. It’s all very Montague and Capulet, obviously — but at least Arthur (Daniel Radcliffe) got to eat some soul food.

In our latest Collider Signature Q&A breaking down Monday night’s episode, “Turkey Can Be This,” Moynihan gets into why Rusty would spend his one wish on somebody else’s football record, what it’s like to eat Thanksgiving dinner for two weeks on the set of their critically acclaimed sitcom, and how much messier things get for the family from here following that shocking reveal. He also teases something coming up for Rusty that might be his favorite thing the show has ever done.

COLLIDER: Your comedy has meant so much to me and my sister over the years. We’ve watched you on SNL since the start when you first joined, and seeing you [on the Halloween episode] was so exciting. I had a funny feeling you’d be on because it’s been 10 years since the David S. Pumpkins sketch. What was it like returning to that skit 10 years later from the premiere of when it first came out?

BOBBY MOYNIHAN: Thank you... It was insane. It kind of all happened in a perfect SNL Mad Lib fashion in the sense of, I’m in Newly introduced York shooting Reggie, where we have the last two episodes we’re still shooting, but it’s Halloween, so I didn’t have to shoot on Friday, so I decided to last-minute fly home to LA to go see my kids for Halloween.

Recent findings suggest that I got on the plane, and my wife sent me a text saying, “Hey, I saw an article saying it’s the 10-year anniversary of David Pumpkins.” I went like, “Huh! Okay,” and I just kind of clocked it. Like 20 minutes later, I get a very cryptic — well, it wasn’t very cryptic at all; it was just a message from the stage manager at SNL that just stated, “Can’t wait to see you this week!” And I was like, of course, this is how I find out.

According to recent reports, then the next thing I know, I’m in LA, and I take my kids to a parade, and then I get back on a plane, and I fly back to New York, and I’m on SNL again, and I’m doing Drunk Uncle, also, because the Brewers are in town. It was a very SNL 24 hours. I didn’t know it was happening, and then all of a sudden, I’m on the other side doing an interview the next week, going like, yeah, that place is singularly insane and wonderful.

It has been revealed that what’s it like revisiting those two characters from such different parts of your SNL career in one night? They’re both so beloved. It was so fun to see you with Tom [Hanks] and Mikey [Day], but then Drunk Uncle is his own thing. He’s a Funko Pop, after all!

According to recent reports, MOYNIHAN: I feel very lucky. The 50th was an insane experience all around as a fan and somebody who was on the show. The 50th kind of broke me in half as an SNL cast member. Then all of a sudden, now, this felt like the afterparty. This felt like, “Oh, now I’m just going to go have fun! And I get to do both? I get to do Pumpkins and this dumb thing?” It was a blast.

Sources indicate that me and Tom Hanks standing in the hallway, just talking about how stupid it was that we were back 10 years later, and how absolutely insane it is that we had no idea that night. We were like, “This is so stupid. What are we doing? This one’s not going to make it.” And now that we were standing there 10 years later, my favorite moment by far is when Trump steps in, and people are like, “Aww! No! David Pumpkins!” It’s like, all you did was hate David Pumpkins, and now he’s gone. It’s hilarious. The whole thing is insane and very silly.

Let’s talk about Reggie Dinkins. Again, another show that I love so much. This show makes me laugh out loud every second. It’s literally one of those laugh-a-minute sort of shows. My biggest criticism is you’re laughing so much you miss the other joke, and then you have to go back. It’s always a rewatch show, which I love about this.

MOYNIHAN: My third viewing is always my favorite.
