Recent findings suggest that courtney Love has praised Tracy Marander – Kurt Cobain‘s one-time girlfriend and photographer behind Bleach‘s album cover – as the “unsung hero” of Nirvana following announcements she is entering hospice and suspending treatment for her cancer. Marander’s family launched a GoFundMe last week to finance her medical bills at her request. As of Monday afternoon, the GoFundMe has raised over $80,000.

Industry observers note that “In the early years, [Tracy] gave Kurt a home and all the space in the world to make music. She believed in him before he believed in himself,” Love wrote on Instagram. “The medical bills have piled up. The American medical system is broken. Give what you can.”.

Recent findings suggest that marander’s husband, Matt Estrada, defended Love from comments under the post saying she should donate a large sum to the fundraiser. “It’s not her responsibility … Technically, it’s ours,” he wrote. “[Tracy] didn’t want to saddle us with these bills after she’s gone. So, if people want to chip in that’s fine. It’s nobody’s responsibility; not Courtney’s, not Dave [Grohl]’s, not Krist [Novoselic]’s, certainly not Frances [Bean Cobain]’s (as I have unbelievably seen as well), and not even yours. But if you chip in, we appreciate it.” Trending Stories Watch Taylor Swift Surprise Brenda Lee With ‘Rockin’ Around the Christmas Tree’ Honor Miley Cyrus and Maxx Morando Marry at Palm Springs Wedding Patrick Stewart Cause of Death Revealed Previously Unseen Footage of Led Zeppelin at Madison Square Garden Surfaces After 49 Years.

According to the GoFundMe, Neko Case, Girl Trouble, record executive Todd Moscowitz, and more are among the reported donors, though a series of anonymous donations ranging from $1,000 to $6,500 top the web fundraiser.

It has been revealed that “[Tracy] is an INCREDIBLE person and a wonderful, real friend to people,” Case wrote on her Substack. “Her family is going to be mired with massive medical bills after she passes and it would be such a kindness to take such worry of her plate in her final days. The GoFundMe is going well so let’s get her to the finish line, shall we?”.

There's something exhilarating about capturing your world from a bird's eye view. With how far drones have come in the last decade, it's now easier than ever to capture such sights — and you don't need to be an expert, either.

Though more deals are yet to come, I've already found killer discounts on my top-rated quadcopters from DJI, Antigravity and HoverAir. The best deal you can get right now is on the Antigravity A1 Explorer Bundle, which is a whopping $660 off at Amazon. This is a fantastic 360-degree drone that lets you capture every angle possible.

Want something a bit more straightforward? The DJI Flip (with RC 2 controller) is down to its lowest ever price of $449 at Amazon, and it's a phenomenal beginner-friendly and lightweight drone for taking traveling with you. There are more deals to take advantage of, of course, so keep reading for the seven best deals on my favorite drones!

According to recent reports, the DJI Flip is a solid mid-range drone, perfect for those looking to upgrade from older DJI models. It captures detailed 48MP stills in all lighting conditions, and records gorgeous 4K/60fps footage. It’s great for content creators as it features many shooting modes, plus it’s built really well and sports a slick design. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller.

The DJI Avata 360's twin lenses let you capture every angle possible, and footage is captured at 8K/60fps, giving you plenty of headroom in post-production. The drone is extremely easy to fly with either goggles or a standard controller, and unlike its primary competition, the Avata 360 does so without breaking the bank. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller, a landing pad, a microSD card, and a backpack.

Industry observers note that with omnidirectional obstacle avoidance and forward-facing LiDAR, the DJI Mini 5 Pro is capable of returning home even without GPS. It introduces a few notable upgrades as compared to its predecessor: a 1-inch sensor for improved low-light performance, 225° gimbal rotation, all while retaining a compact form factor. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller, extra batteries, a landing pad, a microSD card, and more.

It has been revealed that the DJI Mavic 4 Pro records 6K/60fps video and captures 100MP stills powered by a Hasselblad camera. This bundle includes the RC 2 touchscreen controller, a microSD card, a landing pad, and more.

The Antigravity A1 is fitted with tech you’ll find in Insta360's action and 360° cameras, and it lets you capture every angle possible. Flying the drone is easy (and immersive) with the Vision goggles and Grip controller. The Explorer Bundle includes goggles, controller, extra batteries, and more.

If you want a cheaper option, the Antigravity A1 Follow Me Bundle is a great choice. It comes with propeller guards so the drone can fly safely, and a Watch Remote with touch controls for, well, controlling the A1's settings. One-tap cinematic shots are made easy with this bundle.

It has been revealed that unlike most other drones, you don't need a controller or a smartphone to fly the HoverAir X1, which is why it's a great selfie drone. Simply press the buttons on its body and it will record short-form videos and save them internally. My colleague enjoyed using it a lot and appreciated its surprisingly good obstacle avoidance and subject tracking features such as follow, rocket, and more.

Apple has released iOS 27.3 public beta 2 for iPhone. Today’s release also includes a new build for iOS 27.3 beta 2 for developers. The patch brings new Calendar controls, more Siri AI capabilities, and new features for iPhone Duo. It also includes the redesigned Health app and other changes introduced earlier this month.

The patch follows yesterday’s second developer beta and the first public beta on November 5.

Here are the latest changes to try:.

Apple has also detailed higher daily usage limits for Siri AI and other Apple Intelligence features through eligible iCloud+ plans. Plans with 200GB or more include extra capacity; the 50GB plan keeps standard limits.

See our full iOS 27.3 beta 2 roundup for more on the latest discoveries.

The first public beta brought back the redesigned Health app after its earlier preview during iOS 27.2 testing. On iPhones with Apple Intelligence support, Insights collects trends across your health data, while Longevity includes a Health Age comparison based on Apple Watch measurements.

Other changes already available include:.

If you’re already testing the public beta, open Settings > General > Software Update to check for the upcoming version.

According to recent reports, joining for the first time? Make a backup, then enroll in the free Apple Beta Software Program using your iPhone’s Apple Account. In Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, choose iOS 27 Public Beta. Go back to Software Update to download and install it.

It has been revealed that two weeks after premiering its third season, The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power is still the number one show on Prime Video. An epic fantasy drama inspired by J.R.R. Tolkien’s Middle-earth canon, the show is one of the most ambitious TV highlights ever made, with the latest season earning a lot of praise from critics so far. But that said, it’s hardly the only great series you could watch on the platform. Here’s a look at three great shows that we think you should binge this week on Prime Video.

According to recent reports, developed by Peter Harness and Guy Ritchie, Young Sherlock is a series adaptation of Andrew Lane’s books that reimagines Sir Arthur Conan Doyle’s legendary detective as an unruly 19-year-old, years before he became famous. The series follows Sherlock as a student at Oxford University, where he befriends James Moriarty, and they set out to solve his first-ever murder mystery tied to a global-level conspiracy. Hero Fiennes Tiffin stars as Holmes, Max Irons as his brother Mycroft, and Dónal Finn as Moriarty, with Natascha McElhone and Holly Cattle as notable characters.

Created by Matthew Parkhill, Young Sherlock is a youthful, Victorian-era reimagining of English literature’s most iconic detective and a fun pastiche of the Sherlock Holmes canon with a touch of that characteristic Guy Ritchie flair. The show excels as an independent story and is commendable for how it never attempts to recreate Conan Doyle’s original work or draw directly from the original canon. Since its premiere in March 2026, Young Sherlock has been positively received by fans and critics alike, earning praise for Tiffin and Finn’s performances, with the latter cited as a breakout star of the show.

In a recent development, A great detective is really just a personality with a method attached, which is why we keep remaking the same four of them. Here is yours, what it says about you, and the case for them being the best in the business.

You let people think you are not a threat and then you simply never go away. Columbo is the only major detective show that tells you who did it in the first ten minutes, because the pleasure was never the puzzle, it was watching a rich man slowly realise he is in trouble.

You are the most interesting person in the room and you know exactly how to use it. Rian Johnson built Blanc as a gentleman detective who is also an outsider everywhere he goes, which lets him be charming at people who would never otherwise talk to him.

Everybody tells you everything, and you have never once asked them to. Jessica Fletcher is a crime novelist from a small town in Maine who is so warm and so obviously trustworthy that suspects confess to her essentially as a social courtesy.

Recent findings suggest that you expect to be lied to and you are almost never disappointed. Chandler wrote Marlowe as a man with a rigid private code in a city that has none, which is why he takes the case, solves it, gets nothing out of it and takes the next one.

A cult hit teen sports drama created by Peter Berg, Friday Night Lights is a series adaptation of Berg’s 2004 film of the same name, which in turn was inspired by a 1990 book of immersive journalism by H.G. Bissinger. Set in a small fictional town in West Texas, the five-season series follows a high school football team, exploring how their highs and lows affect the close-knit community. The show stars Kyle Chandler, Connie Britton, and Aimee Teegarden in central roles.

According to recent reports, during its run, Friday Night Lights became a critical favorite and built quite a following, but it never quite received the widespread attention it deserves. The series has since amassed an enduring fan base and is considered one of the most well-written television dramas ever. Praised for the compelling performances and grounded portrayal of contemporary Americana, Friday Night Lights is easily one of the finest football shows of all time.

Developed by Scott Neustadter and Michael H. Weber as a musical drama adaptation of the novel by Taylor Jenkins Reid, Daisy Jones & The Six follows the rise and fall of the rock band in 1970s Los Angeles, led by the titular singer-songwriter. The series chronicles their phenomenal growth within the LA music scene, becoming one of the most famous bands in the world, before they split at the height of their success. Riley Keough and Sam Claflin play the lead roles and perform original songs, with Camila Morrone, Suki Waterhouse, Will Harrison, Josh Whitehouse, and Sebastian Chacon starring as the other band members.

Presented in a documentary style with footage of interviews, concerts, and recording sessions, Daisy Jones & the Six feels more realistic than many of its real counterparts. Even though it alters several character arcs, plotlines, and character relationships, the series successfully brings life to the Latest York Times bestseller and is a well-made modern show set in the '70s. Critics have praised the show’s original songs and the musical performances, especially the duets by the leading duo.

I kept waking up at 3a.m. until I changed this simple but hidden iPhone setting — now the dark evenings aren’t ruining my sleep

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • My sleep really took a toll when the clocks fell back this year.
  • I spend a lot of time on my phone both socially and for work and those hours of screen time can have a negative impact on my sleep.
  • I've found that by amending the color of my screen I can mitigate some of the ill-effects that phone use can have — like waking up at night.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

My sleep really took a toll when the clocks fell back this year. I was feeling agitated at bedtime, waking up at 3 a.m., and feeling groggy when my alarm clock went off. That was until I looked at how I was spending my evenings — bathing in the blue glow of my phone as I scrolled into the night.

I spend a lot of time on my phone both socially and for work and those hours of screen time can have a negative impact on my sleep. However, I have stumbled upon a free iPhone setting that has helped me sleep through the night.

I've found that by amending the color of my screen I can mitigate some of the ill-effects that phone use can have — like waking up at night. I caught up with board-certified physician Dr. John La Puma whose work delves into modern exhaustion and how food, light and outdoor protocols impact it.

As a sleep writer I'm precious about my bedtime routine. I begin with a dark shower, make a herbal tea, and get into bed by 9 p.m. without fail most nights. But, as the evenings got darker and I began spending more time indoors, I found it harder to shut off to sleep and experienced more fragmented sleep through the night, no matter how well I thought I was preparing to rest.

Industry observers note that I'd be tossing and turning and then wide awake at 3 a.m. which made for some pretty grumpy mornings. So I was determined to find the cause (and solution) to save my rest this winter.

According to recent reports, eventually, I pinpointed the change in my routine: increased screen time in the evenings. Whereas in the summer I tend to spend the evenings outdoors, as the nights got darker and longer, I was passing more time glued to emails, chatting in the group chat, or hooked on Instagram reels.

Surrendering to the fact I'm not going to eliminate all evening screen time, I've made it my mission to minimise the affect my iPhone has on my sleep. Alongside Wind Down and Sleep Schedule, I recently found the Apple's Night Shift mode.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

In a recent development, this setting automatically adjusts the colors of your display to the warmer end of the spectrum. Instead of bright white light, it shows a warmer tone, making the display easier on your eyes.

Dr. La Puma explains bright, blue-rich light has the biggest impact on tricking your brain into staying awake and alert. So, swapping this for a dimmer, warmer light should make you feel sleepier in the evenings, prevent cortisol spikes, and improve overall sleep outcomes.

"Your brain reads evening light as daytime".

But he says, it's important to dim your screen in the evening as well as putting on Night Shift mode (the mode only changes the tone of the light; it doesn't tamper with the actual brightness level.).

This isn't my first brush with Apple's sleep features. I've already set up my Sleep Schedule, turned on Sleep Focus, and made sure I get a reminder to prioritise sleep at 9:45 p.m. every night (15 minutes prior to my desired sleep time). However, the Night Shift mode is super useful now the evenings are darker and longer. It helps mitigates the effect of that bright white light I'd get from my phone between sundown and bedtime.

It has been revealed that activating Apple Night Shift is simple. Head to your iPhone settings app. Locate 'Display & Brightness' tab. Click into 'Night Shift' and toggle on 'Scheduled'.

Sources indicate that you can then choose to set a custom schedule – so it turns on between 7 p.m. and 7 a.m., for example – or automate the schedule to the actual sunset and sunrise. This way your screen will change as soon as the sunsets and return to white light when the sunrises.

There's also options to manually enable Night Shift, and you can adjust your color temperature. Switch it one manually and you'll immediately see the difference it makes to your screen.

It has been revealed that but there are two precautions from Dr. La Puma. First, "Night Shift warms the color of the screen. It does not dim it, and brightness matters as much as color.".

Switch on Night Shift, then also "turn brightness all the way down" and "put the phone in another room an hour before bed," advises the Californian sleep doctor. "That is what helps.".

Second, he says, "What you are reading or watching keeps you alert too." Whether it's fast paced TikToks or overwhelming news feeds, the content you consume around bedtime can keep your mind ticking when it should be winding down.

Therefore, it's worth considering that late night stimulation for relaxing sleep sounds (our sleep writer, Frances Daniels, has been enjoying Apple's free sleep sounds feature lately) or guided meditations.

Sources indicate that it's just light, how harmful can it be to your sleep? Well, light is actually a key in your circadian rhythm. It has the power to reset your body clock in the mornings and delay sleep onset in the evenings.

Industry observers note that this is all down to the hormone cycles it controls. Bright light suppresses melatonin (the hormone that makes you feel sleepy) and increases cortisol (the hormone that makes you feel alert.) Therefore, too much bright light exposure around bedtime can cause 3 a.m. cortisol spikes, forcing you awake.

Recent findings suggest that spending too much time exposed to bright artificial light in the evenings can cause sleep problems because, as Dr. La Puma explains, "Your brain reads evening light as daytime." As such, it will suppress sleep-inducing hormones.

Industry observers note that "Light reaches melanopsin cells in the retina, which signal the master clock to hold back melatonin. Bright, blue-rich light from overhead LEDs and screens does this most," he indicates.

A 2011 study in the Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism found even ordinary room light before bed delayed melatonin and shortened its night by about 90 minutes. The result? "You feel wired at bedtime, fall asleep later and sleep more lightly," explains Dr. La Puma, who has written a whole book on how the 'indoor epidemic' can impact our sleep.

Industry observers note that great sleep doesn't always come naturally to everyone. Sometimes you need to tweak your habits and environment to help prepare your body for rest. Dr. La Puma has shared his top tips for giving yourself the best chance of getting quality slumber.

Sources indicate that if you want to take restricting your light consumption a step further, consider investing in some blue light blocking glasses from $15.99 now at Amazon. I've recently purchased some of these and am excited to test how effective they are. Early research in the Therapeutic Advances in Ophthalmology Journal indicates promise in their ability to help protect sleep quality.

The best sunrise alarm clock you can buy, the Hatch Sleep Clock is the ultimate gadget for regulating your circadian rhythm. By evening, a warm-toned sunset simulation sends you to sleep. By morning, gradually brightening light wakes you up. Now Black Friday sleep sales are here, you can grab $62.50 off the Hatch Sleep Clock. Just prepare to pay a $4.99/month subscription fee to access all features.

I've spoken about swapping scrolling for reading around bedtime and the hooga red light clip will come in handier than you think. Easily clipping on your book, it helps promote melatonin production and means you needn't get up to turn off a lamp when you feel sleepy. Trust me, it's $12.99 wisely spent.

#154268. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2902 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

📅 09 Feb 2022 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2902 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big challenges.
  • Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.
  • Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big challenges.

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Sources indicate that andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he states he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

It has been revealed that ng’s current efforts are focused on his firm Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to major challenges in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

Recent findings suggest that the great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having noted that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

In a recent development, ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a upcoming paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Industry observers note that ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Recent findings suggest that having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing firm with millions of people.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from major data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI.

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and stated, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

I expect they’re both convinced now.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing latest here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”.

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Recent findings suggest that ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and noted, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one organization or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that indicated up.

Recent findings suggest that you often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from substantial data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

It has been revealed that when you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand upcoming model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For substantial data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng.

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very swiftly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Sources indicate that could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. Fresh tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

It has been revealed that one of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

It has been revealed that ng: In AI, data cleaning is crucial, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention swiftly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

Recent findings suggest that for example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an notable tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

According to recent reports, ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

It has been revealed that “In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion customers. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng.

Industry observers note that synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these challenges more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

According to recent reports, one of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

According to recent reports, ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift matter. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and upgrade the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

It has been revealed that in the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion owners. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

It has been revealed that ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent fresh neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s vital for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

It has been revealed that ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Several decades after World War II ended, this harrowing historical occurrence has remained an important part of modern global discourse. Thanks to the media, we're constantly given a front-row seat to bits and pieces of the event that arguably had the most influence in shaping our world as we know it today. The year so far has delivered its fair share of acclaimed WWII projects, from Tom Hanks' World War II with Tom Hanks docu-series to Brendan Fraser's Pressure and, more recently, Netflix's The Mosquito Bowl, starring Bill Skarsgård. A couple more titles are still expected before the year winds down, but unfortunately, the most anticipated one is missing from that list.

Recent findings suggest that back in 2022, the BBC brought its audiences what would instantly be deemed one of the greatest WWII series since Steven Spielberg and Hanks' miniseries, Band of Brothers. Band of Brothers was a masterclass in TV-making that drew comparisons to another legendary work, Saving Private Ryan, thanks to its high production value and visceral depiction of wartime horrors. Several follow-up efforts to recapture its essence were released to mixed to average reception until the BBC premiered SAS: Rogue Heroes. Created by Steven Knight (Peaky Blinders), SAS: Rogue Heroes has earned universal acclaim, with a rare 100% critic score on Rotten Tomatoes for Seasons 1 and 2.

Sources indicate that season 3 had been in production for some time, and reports of an early 2026 wrap had fans wishing for a late 2026 return. However, it's now official that the acclaimed war series will follow its usual Fresh Year's release window, with the BBC officially reporting that SAS: Rogue Heroes Season 3 will be released in 2027. Alongside the announcement came first-look stills at what to expect from Season 3. The new photos, which can be seen below, feature a host of returning characters including Paddy Mayne (Jack O’Connell), Reg Seekings (Theo Barklem-Biggs), Jim Almonds (Corin Silva), Pat Riley (Jacob Ifan), Bill Fraser (Stuart Campbell) and John Tonkin (Jack Barton).

According to recent reports, season 3 of the series, adapted from Ben Macintyre's best-selling non-fiction book, will pick up from the events of the Season 2 finale, which saw the gallant SAS heroes parachuting towards Nazi-occupied France. The newly introduced chapter opens in the summer of 1994 in France, where they have now landed deep behind enemy lines to destroy the German forces and repel Allied advances. The brave men will yet again confront insurmountable challenges in their mission to free Western Europe.

They will team with the French resistance, as well as members of the Maquis, to be played by a upcoming cast including Bérangère McNeese (Miles & Juliette) and Hélie-Rose Dalmay (The Intruder). Other newcomers arriving in Season 3 include the characters Reverend Fraser McLuskey (Lorne MacFadyen) and an American soldier named Silus Roe, to be played by Nick Hargrove (American Primeval); all of whom can be spotted in the gallery above.

SAS: Rogue Heroes Season 3 will premiere on the BBC and BBC iPlayer on a yet-to-be-announced 2027 date, likely in January, and will stream in the US on MGM+. Stay tuned for future updates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bloomberg reports that Apple is hiring engineers to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of browsing the web, writing code, and controlling apps on behalf of consumers. Here are the details.

In a report published today, Bloomberg notes that new job listings on Apple’s website indicate the firm’s efforts to develop an autonomous AI agent capable of performing complex tasks on the user’s behalf.

Since the breakout success of OpenClaw, autonomous AI agents have become increasingly popular, with companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, and SpaceXSI among those offering their own solutions.

The increasing popularity of these agents has put Apple under pressure to catch up, while the tech giant has also introduced latest restrictions on how third-party AI agents can access and control Macs.

Last month, Apple declared intends to tighten macOS privacy controls around Full Disk Access, with changes introduced in the macOS 27.3 beta that give people more granular control over which apps and information third-party AI agents can access.

Over at the App Store, Meta’s Muse has become one of the fastest-growing apps in US history, surpassing 10 million downloads in just 40 days, according to Sensor Tower, and spending weeks at the top of the charts. As of today, it sits at No. 2 among free apps, behind TikTok.

And while there are differences in how phone-based and computer-based agents operate, these systems can usually work together, coordinating tasks across devices and apps to accomplish increasingly complex goals.

Back to Bloomberg’s report, it notes Apple recently posted new job listings that offer a closer look at its looks to develop autonomous AI agents:.

In one, Apple stated it’s seeking a senior engineering manager for a proactive, agentic AI assistant. The system will write code, browse the web, control apps and navigate devices on a user’s behalf, according to the post.

One job listing, which is for “Senior Engineering Manager, Agentic AI – Proactive,” features the following summary:.

Industry observers note that “Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does. It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple. Our team is building the foundation for that future, and we’re looking for a senior engineering leader to make it real.”.

The listing also notes that Apple is building agents that can “initiative and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way,” much like existing solutions from frontier AI labs.

Industry observers note that today’s report on the newly introduced job listings comes just days after Bloomberg reported that Apple wants to make Siri more like an autonomous AI agent, with the ability to proactively carry out tasks without requiring consumers to initiate every step. According to Mark Gurman, the tech giant could introduce these capabilities as soon as next year.

With the newly introduced job listings, Apple has offered a more detailed look at its plans for autonomous AI agents, although the language suggests that development is still in its early stages.

Of course, given how promptly the technology is evolving, the landscape could look very different by the time Apple is ready to introduce its own solution next year, much like how the industry had already moved toward autonomous agents by the time Apple finally released its long-awaited Siri AI overhaul.

According to recent reports, after releasing developer beta 2 of macOS 27.3 earlier this week, the firm is now rolling out the public beta for users looking to try the new features ahead of next month’s official release. Here’s what’s coming.

Last Monday, Apple released macOS 27.3 beta 2, with newly introduced privacy controls for Full Disk Access and automation tools, and the availability of Apple Intelligence in China.

Those came alongside several new features and tools on macOS 27.3 beta 1, including vertical tabs and adaptive dark mode in Safari, native Live Activities support, Markdown rendering in Quick Look, additional checks for potentially harmful content shared through iCloud links, and Siri AI support for Traditional Chinese, Norwegian, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

Industry observers note that and speaking of Siri AI, macOS 27.3 also expands the assistant’s capabilities across Apple’s own apps, allowing users to perform more complex actions in Messages, Music, Calendar, Photos, and Reminders, as well as manage files and folders. Apple is also introducing new tools for third-party developers to build more advanced Siri AI integrations using Markdown-based instructions.

While macOS 27.2 was a rather uneventful update, macOS 27.3 is shaping up to be the biggest update since the release of macOS 27, and consumers on the public beta can now try out these newly introduced features ahead of their official release.

The release build for macOS 27.3 public beta 2 is 26C5047e, which matches the developer build.

If you’d like to join Apple’s free public beta program, visit beta.apple.com.

Did you spot anything new in today’s beta? Let us know in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a 10-page ruling from the Second Circuit Court of Appeals, the justices found that the 2024 lawsuit filed by Tuff City Records against Universal Music Publishing failed to state a viable claim. The ruling found that the two songs “are not substantially similar as a matter of law.”.

“The works as a whole are distinct,” the ruling obtained by Rolling Stone reads. “The songs differ in their lyrics, melody, genre, subject matter, and overall sound.”.

Sources indicate that the Honey Drippers released “Impeach the President” in 1973, and it rapidly became a Nixon-era protest anthem with a distinctive drum break that would become widely sampled by artists including Janet Jackson, J. Cole, and Doja Cat.

In filing its appeal, Tuff City argued that the lower court used an incorrect legal standard to compare “Real Love” with “Impeach the President.” The appellate court disagreed.

“While ‘Impeach the President’ and ‘Real Love’ share certain percussive elements, other elements are notably different, such as open versus closed hi-hats and distinct snare and kick drum rhythms,” the ruling states. “The songs’ ‘total concept and overall feel’ reinforce the conclusion that the works at issue are not substantially similar.”.

Agreeing with the district court, the ruling found that “Impeach the President” is a protest song that “fits squarely within the soul/funk genre,” whereas “Real Love” is a “hip-hop soul song about heartbreak, not politics.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century.

According to recent reports, hillel I. Parness, a lawyer for Tuff City, stated the organization was “very disappointed” by Monday’s ruling and “will be seeking further judicial review.” He described “Impeach the President” as one of the “most widely- and consistently-sampled songs from the classic hip-hop era” and warned that the decision could have far-reaching implications for the genre. Lawyers for Universal did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech Report: This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos.
  • Recent findings suggest that in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity.
  • Sources indicate that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

Recent findings suggest that in this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

Sources indicate that to buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you stated) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.).

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.).

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

According to recent reports, you’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

In a recent development, but this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.).

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

Every time I test a new Nvidia RTX Spark laptop, I’m looking for the sweet spot — that magical balance where the local AI horsepower, creator muscle and genuine portability finally shake hands. On paper, the Asus ProArt P14 looks like it cracked the code.

Asus managed to crame Team Green’s monster chip into the lightest 14-inch ProArt chassis it has ever built, measuring just 0.55 inches thin and tipping the scale at 3.26 pounds.

Add in a jaw-dropping 3K Lumina Pro OLED touchscreen, a proper SD card reader (no dongle circus required), surprisingly good speakers and a 12.5-hour battery life, and you have a machine that feels effortlessly refined the second you slip it into a backpack.

Industry observers note that I genuinely wanted this to be my favorite RTX Spark laptop. In terms of size, weight, ergonomics, and sheer screen quality, it arguably is.

But physics always collects its debt. To keep a 14-inch chassis this slim and squeeze out 12.5 hours away from an outlet, Asus had to rein in the total wattage. The result is a laptop that can cook your crotch in lap use — especially with its wide, exposed bottom vents — and trails larger RTX Spark machines when you really push the silicon.

And at $3,099 (£3,199), that compromise is a tough pill to swallow unless portability is your absolute number-one priority.

Despite its ultraportable dimensions, this is a desk-or-table machine when you’re doing anything heavier than web browsing.

There’s no polite way to say it: $3,699 is a massive chunk of change for the better RTX Spark, especially for a 32GB unified memory configuration that doesn’t run its headline silicon at full tilt.

Sources indicate that as we’re seeing across all Spark systems, you’re paying a hefty early-adopter fee, but here there’s a miniaturization tax too. If you don’t explicitly need 14-inch portability, that same budget gets you significantly more raw headroom in a larger chassis.

According to recent reports, I really wanted the Asus ProArt P14 to be my favorite RTX Spark laptop. And in a lot of ways, it genuinely is. The 14-inch size, lightweight ergonomics, full port selection, loud speakers, battery life and dazzling 3K OLED panel make it one of the most likable portable creator laptops I’ve used all year.

The rub is that it simply isn’t the fullest representation of what Nvidia’s RTX Spark can do. To make this compact footprint work, Asus had to leave some performance on the table.

Industry observers note that so this leaves it to one particular kind of person — someone like me: a traveling creative or developer who values a compact 14-inch frame and a gorgeous OLED screen above raw benchmark dominance. If you fit in that camp (and your budget can stomach the price), you’re going to love living with this machine.

If you want every single drop of muscle that Spark promises, skip the shrink ray and buy a bigger system.

In a recent development, oh and P.S. Asus (hi if you’re reading this), for the next P14, maybe think about making the frame a touch thicker. That additional thermal headroom would be huge.

He has previously written for Laptop Mag, Tom's Hardware, Kotaku, Stuff and BBC Science Focus. In his spare time, you'll find Jason looking for good dogs to pet or thinking about eating pizza if he isn't already.

Industry News: Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

In a recent development, website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all customers, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but states you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection.".

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a fresh window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

Recent findings suggest that I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

According to recent reports, for something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

According to recent reports, I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Industry observers note that maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Sources indicate that bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.
